title: A machine publishes its workspace record when an agent READS the ledger, not on a session-start timer and never from a child process
context: The superseded decision refreshed the ledger from an unref'd 30s timer at MCP session start, first by spawning a detached `hunch workspaces snapshot` child. On Windows CI that child (and its git subprocess) outlived the MCP session and held a test clone's directory open: team-matrix-e2e's rmSync teardown failed with EBUSY (run 35190856782, job 105102951835, orphan node+git processes in the runner cleanup log). Moving the timer in-process removed the orphan but kept a narrower race — killing the server mid-`git` can orphan git on Windows — and still wrote into the overlay of any unrelated MCP test running longer than the delay.
decision: There is no session-start refresh. The `hunch_workspaces` MCP tool publishes the observation its own read just took (`recordWorkspaceSnapshot(store, root, { live })`, reusing the snapshot via the pure `withPublishMode` so git is not walked twice), in the server process, through the ordinary capture funnel. No timer, no child process, nothing that can outlive the session or hold a directory open. `HUNCH_WORKSPACE_REFRESH=0` makes the call read-only. The git hooks (post-checkout, post-commit) remain the normal refresh path; this covers a host that has no hooks yet.
consequences: The machines that ask about the ledger are exactly the machines visible in it — the one moment the data provably matters.
A session nobody asks writes nothing, so no unrelated long-running MCP test can have its overlay written under it.
A machine whose agent never calls the tool and whose hooks were never installed does not publish; `hunch workspaces snapshot` and `hunch init` are the answer.
alternatives_rejected: Detached child at session start (the original) — orphaned node+git processes held a Windows clone open and broke an unrelated test's teardown with EBUSY.
In-process unref'd timer — removes the orphan child but still races the server's own death mid-git on Windows, and writes into any MCP test that runs past the delay.
Gating the timer on a test-runner env var (NODE_TEST_CONTEXT) — undocumented, and it makes production behavior depend on how the process was launched.
No MCP refresh at all — a host with no git hooks would never publish, which is the case cross-machine visibility exists for.
Raising the timer delay — moves the race rather than removing it; any long enough session still hits it.
